en: Moving mightily toward his khan,
It was written that he would come sated.
My elder Karman from Koy,
It was written that he would come slaughtering.
Making the khan tread the land,
It was written that he would bring him.
With venom coursing through his blood,
Shedding blood wherever he struck,
It was written that he would come surging over them.
Making his mastiff narrow-eyed,
It was written that he would come trampling forward.
It was a letter carefully weighed,
The news in the letter was very grave,
It concerned Ebegey and Köböy,
Jeljetpes who delivered the message,
It was exactly his own self,
To every Kyrgyz he encountered,
To give warning beforehand,
To send news to the people,
Contending through generation after generation,
Sending forth battle cries and acclaim,
So they might walk in freedom,
Without leaving the Kyrgyz without descendants,
From the wrathful one’s snare,
From Chyngteñir’s hand,
To the people caught in danger,
Defending them from the merciless host,
From the true monster’s hand,
From the populous treasury and horde,
The people cried aloud without remainder,
A grievous calamity gathered.
Praying that he separate and rescue them,
Exhausting Ermek the marksman,
Praying that he send a stratagem upon the road.
The people’s realm and treasury,
From hardship like that of wandering servants,
Praying that he preserve them in freedom,
The people had many words to say.
As for poor Jeljetpes,
His two eyes became as four,
Wondering what strength might remain,
Breaking apart evenly,
From his two constricted words,
His true soul cried aloud,
Trembling in suffering,
His entrusted life reached its day,
That noble one pulled at the reins,
He lamented before the Creator,
If they fall into the wrathful one’s hands,
Will the people not be slaughtered entirely?
It became a forceful river,
Wondering whether it had diminished,
Alas, the white-kalpak Kyrgyz people,
Caught in dark hardship,
Their heads entangled in hell,
Wondering whether grief had seized their thoughts,
His wrath became known throughout the world,
Because of Chyngteñir’s wrath,
The Kyrgyz were but a small people,
Despairing of all living souls,
It was a day without a breath of wind,
He himself was a true lion,
The sky became his shelter,
He went to both positions,
For the people and for the realm,
One who would sacrifice his head,
His first ancestor was Kyrgyz,
Their blood was joined together,
Their elder brothers were united,
Their maternal kin struggled together,
Their blood and lives were bound together,
The highly honored Jeljetpes,
He himself was the true former one,
He was the eye of the true faithful man,
Knowing the Kyrgyz quarrel,
Thinking with discerning wisdom,
The campaign of raging Tengir,
Remembering the white-kalpak trail,
The time had come for him to speak.
Bearing grief for a full year,
Rather than remain alive in the world,
The time had come when he would not turn back.
The two companions who wrote on birch,
Jeljetpes who came with the message,
The two companions who wrote the account,
Words impossible to leave after being spoken,
What kind of soul mixed with khanly blood,
He had become lord of the city.
The great one returned at the head of this host.
When he heard this news,
Brave Kenen stood astonished.
Letting his people and nation be overrun,
Or had God struck Kenen?
Gathering the heroes,
If he mounted Kermek, none could approach,
Saddling the gray courser,
The spoken words were words of fury,
They were Zhelzhetpes’s words,
Concerning the Kyrgyz of Ala-Too,
Who was Zhelzhetpes in this age?
It was Kenen’s Khizr-blessed time,
He himself was a true traveler,
His dark eyes were like those of the plane tree,
His clear words were true.
Chyng Tengir said he had mounted and set out,
Upon the path of the blue lion,
To ascend the throne in Beijing,
Saying he had acted while surveying the world,
There had been whispers and rumors,
When its appointed time arrived.
Surely God had struck him,
Would his wretched life not survive?
Zhelzhetpes, who stood impartial,
Spoke as a mediator,
And brought exceptional news.
Thus brave Kenen spoke,
With no place to voice his answer,
He sought refuge and did not fire,
A prudent man,
Lord Tengir came to speech,
Turning another matter upside down,
That the enemy was formidable,
He now understood after deep reflection.
The spread that had been calmly covered,
The ill-fated sword of cast iron,
He grew still more formidable.
He bound together the entire people,
The peerless swift horse Kertulpar,
The dark one who straightened arrows,
Equipped with armor no arrow could pierce,
Putting on an arrow-proof coat,
Mounting a steed no arrow could reach,
The gathered host and people fell into turmoil,
The people raised an uproar and grieved,
Preparing the swift argamak horse,
Driving every racer swiftly,
The people rushed about pondering this,
The siege became a restless tumult,
The people stood anxious and bristling.
Then the hero Kenen,
That hero supported by the chosen army,
Had won fame even among a small people,
His first ancestor had been khan,
He ruled a deeply rooted people.
A true padishah, a sea-like hero,
The tiger among the two sons,
You belonged to your people and realm,
Receiving the blessing of the white-bearded elders,
Committing God’s word to heart,
To Ebegey and Köböy, lion-like men,
To become their companion,
For the people descended by God’s will,
To sacrifice himself and die,
As struggle boiled and the affair burned,
Standing bristling like a dark-maned stallion,
Taking the blessing at his waist,
Setting out against the wrathful one,
Straining like a black lion,
With his heroes behind him,
He began his wrath against hardship,
For the white-kalpak Kyrgyz people,
For Ala-Too, like a lion.
For honor and for dignity,
The dear soul, the valiant lion,
He bound and trained him by a hair’s breadth.
Trained like a fierce fighting bird,
Hardened like sun-bright steel,
Standing forward in plain sight,
Parting from the Ala-Too,
Asking the hero and receiving leave to travel,
Taking a considerable force from the Kyrgyz,
Ask no more about the Altai host,
Clad in garments no bullet could pierce,
Mounting a courser beneath him,
Having one who knew lead the way,
Sixty women in embroidered dress,
They trained him while watching in awe.
Despairing of a life of torment,
Their land burned beneath the sunlit world,
Those beside him understood,
All who remained wailed aloud,
Men and women, old and young,
Wondering what would become of their wretched heads.
What the ear heard and the eye saw,
The khagan was a source of bitter grief,
The Chinese people, the ancestral enemy,
Were no people to be cheaply overcome,
Barykgül advanced without yielding,
Saying, “I shall ride down and wage war,”
None returned safely from Maderin.
The khan received it as news,
All the men who served as eyes had died,
The edge of truth had turned back,
All of Chyng’s assembled host,
Was torn from its wretched life.
That enemy, the people of Beijing,
Go safely and return unharmed,
From your wound they will know your affliction,
The world where divine power tests us is false.
Alas, he did not turn back,
Knowing the news, bitter with rage,
The Chinese deed was a hell of venom,
Saying they were Kyrgyz,
All the Chinese fell into turmoil,
He gave his blessing without stirring.
He asked a blessing from the people,
Their ordered ranks were shattered,
He hurled them about like a ball,
Fate’s command was this great,
To see how their designs would turn,
Ebegei stood at the edge of the people,
To Kogoi, the blue-maned elder,
Second among the true Kyrgyz,
To his friends Ebegei and Kogoi,
To consider the broad matter,
For Ebegei and Kogoi to go,
To serve as support and visible strength,
Let Kenen mount without delay.
The earth stirred without breaking,
His journey grew this long,
It was abundant, not slight,
He crossed the dark river valley,
He skirted the black-ridged mountain,
The steeds filled the ravines,
Countless gold adorned them,
Divided into thousands and hundreds,
Their dust struck against dust,
Countless ranks gathered,
They made a host that shook the earth,
My hero Kenen, the blue-maned one,
Making the mountain level beneath him,
Rising toward the sky and halting,
The army surged in alarm and dust,
Spears appeared on every side,
All the heroes divided into ranks,
Their champions rejoiced.
A wrathful man with no tethering post,
A lone sharp-maned hero,
If booty came by chance,
Saying it would strengthen the people,
O brother in the moonless darkness,
Saying it would become night for the people.
The old yellow one came with news,
What happened rank after rank,
To all the hundred thousand servants,
He appeared measuring himself against repentance,
Chagatai mounted the pale-gray horse,
Becoming one with the gray-mounted men,
Girded with black steel,
Gathering courage, he struck firmly,
Binding it firmly in the name of repentance,
Bringing a dream no ninety could take,
Tall of stature and broad of shoulder,
Both a champion and a hero,
The heart of his whole region,
Mounting him at the true place,
